Both, floating

1 exfiltration (NetworkPolicy) · 2 villain image (Kyverno at admission) · 3 the recipe on disk (KubeArmor in the kernel) · 4 denial-of-wallet (budget guard) · 5 the CEO record (output guard) · 6 prompt injection (input guards) · 7 rogue tool (tool allow-list) · 8 the service-account token (a scoped Role).

Challenge 6 and Challenge 7 are the same class of attack stopped by two different kinds of control.
C6 stops the text before the model reads it, and the model never knows it was attacked.

model read everything, be fully persuaded, and find the capability gone.

The other is "it wanted to and could not".
Only the
second still holds when the next model is more persuadable than this one.

How to block data exfiltration attacks in Kubernetes
What is a network policy?
By default, every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can talk to every other pod, and to anything on the public internet.
Nothing is in the way.
That is convenient while you are building something, and alarming once something in the cluster is doing what it was talked into rather than what it was built for.
A network policy is how you say which traffic is allowed.
You write down what a pod may talk to, and everything else is refused.
The refusal happens in the network layer, so the workload does not get an error it can catch and work around.
It simply never connects.
You want one here because the agent has a tool that can make web requests, and a tool that can reach the whole internet can send your data anywhere on it.
Taking the tool away would break the agent's real work.
Deciding where it may send things does not.
This type of attack is called data exfiltration.
Kubernetes has this guardrail built in, as the NetworkPolicy object.
NetworkPolicies are an application-centric Kubernetes construct which allow you to specify how a pod is allowed to communicate with various network “entities”.
NetworkPolicies allow you to specify rules for traffic flow within your cluster, and also between Pods and the outside world.
First, look at what you will apply:

How to fix rogue image deployments
What is a cluster-level policy?
A policy is an organization-specific rule about what actions (like create, update, delete) are allowed to happen on what objects in a system.
An admission controller policy is a rule specifically about what you are allowing into your Kubernetes cluster.
Admission controller policies are helpful in many ways, such as:
Security: for example, ensuring that Pods do not run in privileged mode.
Governance: for example, label every Ingress with a certain label.
Automation: for example, when a new namespace is created, add a ConfigMap in that namespace.
Cost Optimization: for example, there should not be any services of type LoadBalancer in a given namespace.
How an admission controller works
When you create an admission controller policy, two things happen.

First, a webhook is created that teaches the kube-API server that when it sees a request that pairs a certain kind of resource with a certain action (for example, create, update, or delete), the kube-API should send that request somewhere.
This webhook is called an admission controller webhook, and basically, it is configuration for the kube-API server.
Second, the kube-API sends any matching request to the admission controller that configured the webhook.
The admission controller is a piece of software, and the software itself is different depending on what the tech is.
Admission controllers can also be called policy engines.
As a side note, the term admission controller is confusing because unlike other types of controllers in Kubernetes, an admission controller does not run as a reconciliation loop.
Instead, it is activated by the aforementioned admission controller webhooks.
A policy can be validating or mutating.
A validating policy answers yes or no: this action is allowed on this resource, or it is not, and the kube-API acts accordingly.
A mutating policy edits the resource on its way in, before it is validated and stored.
The one you are about to apply is validating.
Kyverno
There are other CNCF projects that do this job: OPA Gatekeeper and Kubewarden.
Some cluster-level policy functionality is also available natively in Kubernetes, as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.
On the Community cluster there is nothing to fix this with.
No admission controller is installed here: no Kyverno, no policy, no webhook.

How to add runtime security to fix filesystem snooping
What is a runtime policy?
Runtime policies protect a system from security vulnerabilities and threats during their execution.
They secure against unknown unknowns at runtime.
How can it possibly watch everything?
All of the applications in a cluster each have so many processes running.
As the estate grows there might be hundreds of thousands or even millions of processes running at once.
How can a runtime security tool even begin to monitor them all?
With runtime security, monitoring is done at the kernel level of each host machine.
That means that runtime security is not application-specific.
A runtime security tool will look at kernel-level events such as a process being executed, a file being opened, something being accessed over the network, or a particular system call being made.
When one is implementing runtime policy, the first step is to monitor these kernel-level events to define expected behavior in the system.
Then one can create a policy that will do something when an unexpected event occurs.
What that something is depends on the tool, and this cluster runs one of each kind.
On the Community cluster, nothing noticed.
There are two kinds of runtime tool, one that detects and one that prevents, and only the prevention engine is installed here.
Falco, the cloud native threat detector, is not on this cluster, so there is no alert to watch for and no log to read.

The prevention half is real.
KubeArmor's engine is running here with no policy loaded, which is why the read worked, and the policy below works on this cluster exactly as written.

How to fix denial-of-wallet attacks
This type of attack is called a denial-of-wallet attack.
The guardrails so far all answer "is this allowed?".
But for this situation, the question we want to answer is "How much usage is allowed by a single user?"
First, what is the guard-proxy?
The guard-proxy is a small piece of software running in your cluster, in the agent namespace, alongside BurritoBot.
It was installed with the rest of the platform when your cluster was built, and it belongs to the platform team, not to the developers who wrote BurritoBot.
It was written for this workshop; the content scanning it does in Challenges 5 and 6 is handed off to LLM Guard, which is an open-source project.
It sits in the request path.
When you send a message it goes to the guard-proxy first.
The guard-proxy decides whether to pass it on to the agent, and when the agent's reply comes back, the guard-proxy sees that too before you do.
Every AI guardrail in this workshop that is not a Kubernetes object lives here: the budget cap you are about to install, the output guard in Challenge 5, and the input guard in Challenge 6.
There is one guard-proxy on this cluster and it fronts one agent.
In a real platform you would run one per agent, so that a limit set for one team's agent does not affect another's.
The fix is a budget cap.
It keeps a running total of spend and refuses once the total crosses the limit.
The check runs before the model is called, so a refused request costs nothing.

# what that does, and what it changes
GET /toggle?budget=on -> GUARDS['budget'] = True
# enforced per request, before the Bedrock call:

refuse() # 0 tokens, 0 cost

Nobody turns a budget cap off in production.
They scope it per customer, so the account running up the bill is the only one that stops.
Every other guardrail you install today behaves the same way: it blocks the bad thing and lets everything else through.

The real thing is many sessions at once: a script, or a botnet, hammering the agent from hundreds of conversations in parallel.

What is output scanning?
A guardrail can sit on either side of the model.

How to fix prompt injection attacks
What is input scanning?
Input scanning is the other half of the pair.
It reads the prompt before the model does, and refuses it if it looks like an attack.
Refusing early is cheaper in every sense.
The model is never called, so the request costs nothing.
Nothing is read, so nothing can leak.
And there is no reply to clean up, because there is no reply.
The hard part is deciding what "looks like an attack" means, and there is no single good answer.
So two different checks usually run together, because they fail in opposite directions.
This is prompt injection.
The model gets one stream of text and cannot reliably tell "content to read" from "instructions to follow".
You asked it to read a ticket, and the ticket did the asking.
Every agent that reads content it did not write has this problem.
The fix is input scanning: a check on what goes into the model before the model reads it.

Two checks run on the prompt itself, because they fail differently:
Block list: matches known-bad strings.

Classifier: a small model trained to spot injection attempts.
Catches new wording, but can be wrong in either direction.

What is a tool allow-list?

How to fix over-privileged credentials
What is RBAC?
Kubernetes decides who may do what with role-based access control, usually shortened to RBAC.
It works the way it sounds.
You write down a set of allowed actions, and you attach that set to an identity.
The set is a Role: a list saying which actions, on which kinds of object, inside one namespace.
Create pods.
Read configmaps.
List secrets.
The attachment is a RoleBinding, which says who the Role applies to.
The identity is the part worth slowing down on, because it is the one nobody chose.
Every pod in Kubernetes runs as a ServiceAccount, and if nobody names one, it gets the namespace default anyway.
A workload does not opt in to having an identity.
It has one, and that identity has whatever the cluster gave it.
You want RBAC scoped tightly because the question is never "is this workload trustworthy".
It is "what could anyone holding this credential do".
Those are different questions, and the second one is the one you just answered from your terminal.
Kubernetes attaches a ServiceAccount to every pod, and if the developer names none it attaches the namespace default.
That attachment is the whole vulnerability.

It projects a bearer token into the container at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, and anything that can read that file can act as the agent, which is what makes the cat in the chat version a theft rather than a diagnostic.
The account was allowed to read any Secret in the namespace, and to list all of them.
It only needs one (the CEO record, for Challenge 5).
The extra reach is what let it dump the terminal password.
The base64 is not encryption and is not protection; the API returns Secret values that way and anyone can decode them.
It is, however, why the output guard from Challenge 5 stayed silent: that guard matches readable text, and there was none to match.
None of the earlier guardrails helped, because they sit between the model and its tools.
This request went straight to the API server, around all of them.
